positions: The Spirit proceeds from the Father (Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox; the text of 381)
The Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son (Roman Catholic, most Protestant churches)
The Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son (formulas used in ecumenical dialogue)
why_inside: All three affirm that the Spirit proceeds from the Father (P18) and is fully divine (P19). The dispute concerns the eternal relations of origin, the authority to amend a conciliar creed, and how the West added the clause; it is serious, but it is a dispute between Trinitarians about the Trinity, not about whether God is Triune.

positions: Two natures in one person (Chalcedonian: Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, most Protestants)
One incarnate nature of God the Word (Miaphysite: Oriental Orthodox)
why_inside: The boundary is set at 381 on purpose. The Oriental Orthodox churches and the Church of the East confess the Creed of 381 but not every later definition. Joint Christological declarations since the 1970s and 1990s have recognised substantial agreement. Choosing 381 rather than 451 keeps them inside.

All confess 'one baptism for the forgiveness of sins' in their own sense. Groups that do not practise water baptism (for example the Quakers and the Salvation Army) are not flagged by Dust; P22 is ecclesial and the layer annotates rather than blocks on it.
The Creed of 381 says nothing about the Eucharist.

topic: Identity and government of the Church
positions: Papal primacy and the Catholic Church as the Church of Christ
The invisible or universal Church across denominations
why_inside: Each tradition confesses 'one holy catholic and apostolic Church' and identifies it differently. Dust does not adjudicate.

positions: Theotokos (affirmed at Ephesus 431 and by many Protestants)
Immaculate conception and assumption (Roman Catholic dogma)
Rejection of Marian dogmas beyond Scripture (many Protestants)
why_inside: The Creed requires only that Christ was incarnate of the Virgin Mary (P10).

positions: Justification by faith alone (Lutheran, Reformed, evangelical)
Justification as infused righteousness through faith and sacraments (Roman Catholic)
Arminian and Wesleyan accounts of grace
why_inside: The Creed confesses that Christ came 'for us and for our salvation' and was 'crucified for us' (P09, P12), but does not define justification. The 1999 Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification records partial agreement. These differences matter to the traditions concerned; Dust presents them fairly and does not decide them.

positions: Scripture and Tradition with the Magisterium
why_inside: The Creed confesses that the Spirit 'spoke through the prophets' and that Christ rose 'according to the Scriptures', without defining the canon or the relation of Scripture to Tradition.
The Creed confesses God as Maker of all things (P02) and the Son as the one through whom all things were made (P08), not the mechanism or timescale.

positions: Views on purgatory, intermediate state, hell (eternal conscious punishment, conditional immortality) and hope for universal reconciliation
why_inside: The Creed requires Christ's return and judgement (P15), an endless kingdom (P16) and the resurrection of the dead (P23). It does not settle the millennium or the details of final destiny. A view is flagged only if it denies return, judgement or resurrection outright.
